lead: The exhaust gas oxygen sensor, also called the lambda sensor, measures oxygen left in the exhaust. The ECU uses it to hold the air-fuel ratio near stoichiometric, where a three-way catalyst works best, or near a target lambda. Petrol stoichiometric AFR is 14.7:1 by mass. The sensor closes the fuel loop: air charge sensors set a base fuel mass, and the EGO trims it. Narrowband sensors switch sharply near λ = 1; wideband sensors give a linear reading. Used on petrol, gas and some diesel engines.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for signal conditioning, 3.2 for air charge, and 3.5 for temperature effects.

blocks.text: Lambda λ is the actual air-fuel ratio divided by the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio for the fuel. For petrol, stoichiometric AFR is 14.7 kg air per kg fuel, written 14.7:1. λ = AFR<sub>actual</sub> / AFR<sub>stoich</sub>. λ less than 1 is rich (excess fuel), λ equal to 1 is stoichiometric, λ greater than 1 is lean (excess air). The same λ can apply to petrol, CNG or ethanol if the correct stoichiometric AFR is used.

blocks.where: AFR<sub>actual</sub> is the actual air-fuel mass ratio; AFR<sub>stoich</sub> is the stoichiometric ratio, 14.7:1 for petrol; λ is dimensionless.

blocks.text: The ECU runs closed-loop fuel trim. Air charge sensors give the base fuel mass. The EGO signal tells the ECU whether the last combustion was rich or lean. Short-term fuel trim multiplies the base injection time. Long-term trim learns the slow offset. Around λ = 1 the narrowband output changes fast, so the ECU can hold the average close to stoichiometric.

The sensor does not measure AFR directly. It measures oxygen partial pressure in exhaust. Rich exhaust has little oxygen because fuel consumes it. Lean exhaust has excess oxygen. The zirconia cell turns that oxygen difference into a voltage.

The narrowband zirconia sensor is an oxygen concentration cell. A thimble of yttria-stabilised zirconia separates exhaust gas from reference air. Porous platinum electrodes cover both sides. Above about 300 °C the ceramic conducts oxygen ions. The voltage follows the Nernst equation.

blocks.where: E is the cell voltage in volts; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is the gas constant; T is absolute temperature in K; F = 96485 C/mol is the Faraday constant; pO<sub>2,ref</sub> is the oxygen partial pressure in reference air; pO<sub>2,exh</sub> is the oxygen partial pressure in exhaust.

blocks.text: In rich exhaust the oxygen partial pressure on the exhaust side is low, so the cell produces about 0.8–0.9 V. In lean exhaust the two oxygen pressures are closer, so the output falls to about 0.1 V. The transition is steep near λ = 1. The ECU sees a switch, not a proportional AFR. This is why the device is called a switching or narrowband sensor. Some syllabi call it lambda sensor, EGO or HEGO (heated exhaust gas oxygen).

A heater inside the sensor brings it to light-off quickly. The ECU controls the heater with pulse-width modulation, often using a power switch; see 3.8. Thimble sensors use a cup-shaped ceramic. Planar sensors stack ceramic layers and electrodes on a flat strip; they heat faster and are smaller. A protective shield and a porous layer protect the electrodes from liquid water and deposits.

Desirable properties: fast light-off, high sensitivity near λ = 1, low hysteresis, resistance to lead and silicone poisoning, and stable heater control. Hysteresis means the rich-to-lean and lean-to-rich switching voltages differ; low hysteresis gives a cleaner switch. Poisoning reduces the active electrode area and slows response.

The wideband universal exhaust gas oxygen (UEGO) sensor gives a linear λ output. It uses a pump cell and a sensing cell. The ECU pumps oxygen into or out of a small chamber to hold the sensing cell at about 450 mV, which corresponds to λ = 1. The pump current needed is proportional to the oxygen excess or deficit in the exhaust. A conditioning circuit converts that current into a linear voltage for the ECU.

Because the pump current is linear, the ECU can read λ over a wide range, roughly from λ = 0.7 up to free air (λ tending to infinity). Petrol direct-injection and diesel engines use wideband sensors for lean operation and for closed-loop control away from stoichiometric. A wideband sensor is not a narrowband sensor with a different connector; it has extra cells and a controller.

Titania (TiO<sub>2</sub>) sensors use a different principle. The electrical resistance of titania changes with oxygen partial pressure. They need a heater because resistance is temperature-sensitive. The ECU measures the resistance as a voltage divider. Titania sensors are less common than zirconia but appear in some systems. Their output also switches near λ = 1 in the simple form.

All EGO sensors sit before or after the catalyst. The upstream sensor controls fuel. The downstream sensor checks catalyst oxygen storage. Catalyst chemistry and emission norms belong to Unit 4, Electronic Engine Control.

figure.caption: Narrowband EGO voltage against lambda. The output is high on the rich side, low on the lean side, and switches sharply through λ = 1.

spec.aria: Line graph of narrowband EGO voltage against lambda, switching sharply near lambda equal to one.

examples.question: A petrol engine has stoichiometric AFR 14.7:1. The exhaust gas oxygen sensor indicates the mixture is at an actual AFR of 15.4:1. Calculate lambda. State whether the narrowband EGO output is high or low and estimate its value from the switching characteristic.
steps: Write the definition: λ = AFR<sub>actual</sub> / AFR<sub>stoich</sub>.
Compare with 1: λ = 1.048 is greater than 1, so the mixture is lean.
Read the narrowband characteristic: a lean mixture near λ = 1.05 gives a low output, about 0.1 V. It does not give a proportional reading of 0.048.
examples.answer: λ = 1.048 (dimensionless), so the mixture is lean; a narrowband EGO output is low, about 0.1 V.
examples.check:
afr_actual = 15.4
afr_stoich = 14.7
lam = afr_actual / afr_stoich
print(f'{lam:.3f}')
print(0.1)

traps: High EGO voltage means rich, not lean. The narrowband output is about 0.9 V on the rich side, at λ less than 1 (for example λ = 0.9), and about 0.1 V on the lean side, at λ greater than 1 (for example λ = 1.1).
A narrowband EGO voltage is not proportional to AFR. Reading 0.45 V as a precise lambda value is wrong; the sensor switches and the ECU uses the switch.
A cold sensor gives no useful signal. Light-off and heater control are part of the sensor system; a heater open circuit sets a fault and forces open-loop fuel.
Lead and silicone poisoning reduce response. Do not confuse poisoning with a rich mixture or a faulty heater.
Wideband pump current is not the same as the Nernst voltage. The sensing cell is held near 450 mV; the pump current carries the λ information.

quiz.q: Define lambda for an engine. State the stoichiometric AFR of petrol by mass.
quiz.a: λ = AFR<sub>actual</sub> / AFR<sub>stoich</sub>; petrol stoichiometric AFR = 14.7:1.

quiz.q: What voltage range does a narrowband zirconia EGO sensor show rich and lean?
quiz.a: About 0.8–0.9 V rich and about 0.1 V lean; it switches near λ = 1.

quiz.q: Why is the narrowband EGO output not a linear AFR signal?
quiz.a: It is a Nernst concentration cell. The voltage depends on the logarithm of the oxygen pressure ratio, and the oxygen pressure changes steeply near λ = 1. The ECU therefore sees a switch.

quiz.q: Actual AFR is 13.2:1. Find λ and state rich or lean and the narrowband output.
quiz.a: λ = 13.2 / 14.7 = 0.898. λ is less than 1, so rich; narrowband output is high, about 0.9 V.

quiz.q: Explain the role of the pump cell in a wideband UEGO sensor.
quiz.a: The pump cell moves oxygen in or out to keep the sensing cell at about 450 mV, which is λ = 1. The pump current is proportional to the exhaust oxygen excess or deficit, giving a linear λ signal.

quiz.q: A used car has slow EGO response. Give two poison species and explain the effect on closed-loop trim.
quiz.a: Lead and silicone. They cover the platinum electrodes, reduce active area and slow switching; fuel trim becomes slow or biased and emissions rise.

quiz.q: Compare thimble and planar narrowband sensors.
quiz.a: Thimble: cup-shaped ceramic with reference air inside. Planar: stacked flat layers, smaller and faster heating, common in modern cars. Both use a zirconia Nernst cell.

quiz.q: Why does the ECU use PWM for the EGO heater?
quiz.a: To control heater power and temperature, give fast light-off, avoid overheating, and reduce losses in the power switch.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems often use a smart wideband sensor with an integrated controller and a digital or current-loop interface. Diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines add NOx and particulate sensors, and model-based air-path control uses lambda together with cylinder pressure. Research looks at fast light-off, low-power heaters and tolerance to sulphur and biofuel deposits. Search next for UEGO pump current, lambda sensor light-off, and lean NOx trap control.
